entities.summary: In astronomy and astrophysics, an ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX) is less luminous than an active galactic nucleus but more consistently luminous than any known stellar process (over 1039 erg/s, or 1032 watts), assuming that it radiates isotropically (the same in all directions). Typically there is about one ULX per galaxy in galaxies which host them, but some galaxies contain many. The Milky Way has not been shown to contain an ULX, although SS 433 is a candidate. The main interest in ULXs stems from their luminosity exceeding the Eddington luminosity of neutron stars and even stellar black holes.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: ULXs have significant implications for our understanding of extreme astrophysical processes and the potential for new discoveries in the field of neutron star physics. The study of ULXs has also shed light on the role of supermassive black holes in galaxy evolution.
